---
title: "How to play"
description: "What Path Tracer is, how the sectors work, and who makes it."
---

**Path Tracer** is a library of short explainer videos on the methods behind biosocial science: how evolution shapes
behaviour, how twins reveal heritability, how genome-wide studies find genes, how penalized regression tames a
million predictors, and how marks on DNA keep biological time.

## The rules of the game

- **Sectors** are the big topics. Each one is a landscape of its own.
- **Levels** are the episodes, 2–7 minutes each. Every level answers one question and ends on the next one.
- **Play a sector in order.** Levels build on each other, and each one says up front which earlier levels it assumes.
- **Legendary** levels are the advanced material at the end of each sector. They open once the core path is clear.
- A level's light tells you where it stands. **Online** levels are released. **In production** levels are being
  built. **Locked** levels are planned, and the map shows them anyway, so you can see where the game is going.

## The style

Two YouTube channels inspired the house style.
[StatQuest](https://www.youtube.com/@statquest) never skips a step, uses tiny examples and marks every payoff.
[3Blue1Brown](https://www.youtube.com/@3blue1brown) treats the picture as the argument and keeps the maths exactly
right. Path Tracer tries for both: every symbol gets a picture before it gets notation, and nothing is simplified into
something false.

The look is *the Grid*, a soft-glow homage to a certain light-cycle film. The name comes from Sewall Wright's
*path tracing*, the rules that turn a diagram of genes and environments into the equations of the twin model. The
light cycle in the videos traces those same paths.

## Who makes it

Peter Tanksley, a research scientist who teaches biosocial criminology. Path Tracer is an evenings-and-weekends
project. The videos are built in [Manim Community Edition](https://www.manim.community/) and this site in
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/).
